User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $650 in work sup

plies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Short answer
- Take the standard deduction (married filing jointly standard deduction for 2023 = $27,700). Your itemizable deductions (you only listed $800 charity) are far below that.
- You can (and should) report your consulting income on Schedule C and deduct the $650 in supplies and a home‑office deduction (only for the consulting work, not for your W‑2 job). That reduces your self‑employ

ment income and lowers both income tax and self‑employment tax.
- Student loan interest (up to $2,500) is an above‑the‑line deduction (you can claim it even though you take the standard deduction) provided your MAGI is below the phaseout range — with your income it looks like you’ll be under the phaseout, so you can take $2,500 of the $2,700 you paid.
- You’ll need Form 1040 plus Schedule C (profit/loss from business), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), and either Form 8829 (regular home‑office method) or u

se the simplified home office method on Schedule C.

Details and numbers (to help choose the home‑office method)
Income you listed:
- W‑2 pay: $84,900
- Consulting: $22,100
- Interest: $920
- Dividends: $195
Total income = $108,115 (before business expense adjustments)

Student loan interest
- Deduction limit = $2,500 (maximum). You paid $2,700; you can deduct up to $2,500 if you meet the income limit.
- The deduction is an adjustment to income (reported on Schedule 1), so it reduces AGI whether or not you

itemize.
- Your total income here is well under the phaseout threshold for 2023, so you should get the full $2,500 (but keep your 1098‑E or payment records).

Charitable contributions
- $800 cash to a qualified charity is an itemized deduction. Because the standard deduction for MFJ (2023) is $27,700, itemizing for $800 doesn’t make sense. Take the standard deduction.

Consulting (self‑employment) items
- Report the $22,100 on Schedule C.
- Deductible business expenses you listed: $650 (work supplies).
- Ho

me office deduction: you can claim either the simplified method or the regular (actual expense) method — only for the portion of your home used exclusively and regularly for your consulting business.

Home office math (you said office = 165 sq ft; home total = 690 sq ft)
- Business portion = 165 / 690 = 23.9% (≈0.239)
- Rent = $2,050/month -> annual rent = $24,600

Regular method (allocating actual home expenses)
- Rent portion deductible = $24,600 × 0.239 ≈ $5,883 (you can also include utilities, renter’s

insurance, etc., pro‑rata).
- Combined with $650 supplies, total business expenses ≈ $6,533.
- Net self‑employment income ≈ $22,100 − $6,533 = $15,567 (positive, so the full home office amount is usable).

Simplified method
- $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 165 × $5 = $825.
- Combined with $650 supplies, total expenses = $1,475.
- Net self‑employment income ≈ $22,100 − $1,475 = $20,625.

Which is better for you?
- Regular method yields a much larger home‑office deduction here (~$5,883 vs $825), so it will lo

wer your taxable/self‑employment income more. Because your regular‑method home office deduction won’t push your Schedule C into a loss, the regular method looks advantageous.
- Use the simplified method if you want minimal recordkeeping and calculation. Use the regular method if you have supporting documentation for rent/utilities and want the larger deduction.

Self‑employment tax and related deduction
- You’ll owe self‑employment tax (Social Security & Medicare) on net Schedule C profit. You calculate thi

s with Schedule SE.
- Half of the self‑employment tax is an above‑the‑line deduction on Schedule 1.
- Net effect: home‑office and supplies reduce your Schedule C profit and therefore reduce both income tax and self‑employment tax.

Forms and where things go (what to file)
- Form 1040 (main return)
- Schedule 1 — reports adjustments to income (student loan interest and the deductible half of SE tax appear here)
- Schedule C — report consulting income and business expenses (supplies, home‑office deduction eit

her via Form 8829 or simplified)
- Schedule SE — compute self‑employment tax
- Form 8829 — use only if you choose the regular home‑office method (to compute allowed business‑use‑of‑home expenses)
- Attach W‑2 and include 1099‑NEC (or other 1099s) for consulting if you received them
- Report interest and dividends on Form 1040 (Schedule B only if interest + dividends > $1,500 or other triggers)

Recordkeeping you should keep
- Receipts for charitable donation (your receipt), 1098‑E from the loan servicer (st

udent loan interest), rent and utility bills (for regular home office method), receipts for supplies, 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC, 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, and copies of your W‑2.
- If you use the regular home office method, keep a floor plan/note showing exclusive business use of that 165 sq ft.

Other points to consider
- Oregon state return: state rules can differ; check Oregon’s rules for the student loan interest deduction and home office treatment or ask your tax preparer.
- Estimated tax / withholding: because you

had self‑employment income, you likely owe additional federal (and state) tax and should make estimated payments for future years if you expect to continue consulting.
- If you want, I can run the numbers more precisely for both home‑office methods and estimate your federal tax and self‑employment tax for 2023 — tell me whether you want the regular (detailed) or simplified home‑office calculation and whether there are any other deductible items (mortgage interest, state/local tax paid, medical expenses, re

tirement contributions, business mileage, other business expenses, etc.).

Bottom line recommendation
- Take the standard deduction ($27,700).
- Report consulting on Schedule C and claim business supplies ($650) and the home office deduction (regular method looks better here).
- Claim $2,500 student loan interest as an above‑the‑line deduction.
- File 1040 + Schedule C + Schedule SE and Form 8829 (if using regular home‑office method).

Would you like me to:
- (A) run a side‑by‑side calculation showing estim

ated taxable income and estimated federal tax under the regular vs simplified home‑office methods, or
- (B) draft an email you can send to your tax preparer with these numbers and questions?
